english: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores, Argentina are world champions.

At the halfway line, the captain hugs his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with his country, and six years ago he quit the national team. The final in Qatar may be his last chance.
As Montiel runs up, the captain looks at the sky, which he points to after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years earlier, doctors in Rosario saw this child was barely growing. So every night, he injected his leg.
Almost four years after Qatar, Argentina played in a World Cup final again. Two days later, he wrote a short note. It contained two Spanish words. Me vacié. I have given everything.
He rarely talks. He just plays. How could a quiet boy who was too small carry a whole country? It all started on a small pitch in Rosario, one afternoon, when a children's team was one player short.
He also thanked his family. Without them, his career would not exist. The first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. The coach, Salvador Aparicio, was looking for anyone who could play.
At the side of the pitch was a woman called Celia. She was watching her grandson, Matías, and had brought his younger brother, a boy of four or five.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and hesitated. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia did not give up. She kept asking for her grandson to be played.
Aparicio finally agreed. He put him on the wing, near Celia, and said: if he cries, take him off.
At first he barely touched the ball. But when the ball came again, he carried it with his left foot and beat opponents one by one. He did not cry. Later he remembered scoring two goals.
In that first game, the other children were two or three years older. Some were twice as big. But it didn't matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. From then on, Celia took him to every practice and game.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked in a steel factory. His mother worked in a small workshop making magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later, his younger sister, María Sol, completed the family.
Rosario is a workers' city on the Paraná River. There are factories, a port, and two clubs that divide it: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in the La Bajada neighbourhood. He and his brothers played in the street until dark. Lionel was always the smallest, and always had the ball.
He went to a state school near home, School Number 66. Later, a mural of his face appeared in the neighbourhood. It says: he comes from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home, everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and quick, family and teammates gave him a nickname. La Pulga. The Flea.
According to his mother, at home he could be naughty and stubborn. He hated losing, even at cards. But on the pitch, that trait made him never give up the ball.
His father and brothers supported Newell's Old Boys, the red-and-black side of the city. Every match, the family went to the stadium together. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six, he joined the family's favourite club, Newell's Old Boys. In an early game, his team won six-nil, he scored four.
The children born in 1987 became a team still talked about in Rosario. Its name was "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of '87. For years, they almost never lost.
Sometimes opposing teams asked for an agreement before the game: if the score reached six-nil, the match would be stopped. Even at six-nil, Lionel was annoyed if he had not scored yet.

Coach Carlos Marconi likes to tell a story. He promised Leo one alfajor, a chocolate biscuit, for each goal. Leo scored too many, so Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, only for headers. Soon the smallest boy scored a header. He turned to Marconi, smiled and held up two fingers.
His teammates remember small things. Before games, he looked after his boots and taped his own ankles, like a pro. He was only eight or nine.
A teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo kept beating the same defender, until the defender's father shouted from the stand: kick him!
The league recorded his goals: more than two hundred in five years. People in Rosario say the real number was much higher.
The small body was always a problem. Big defenders kicked him, some parents shouted: stop him, whatever it takes! He always got up and asked for the ball again.
Coaches wanted to protect him: pass quicker so you don't get injured. He kept dribbling. If he lost the ball, he quickly won it back.
But in 1998, at ten, grandmother Celia died. The person who brought him to football was gone.
Later he said his grandmother was a very great love for him, and even now it is hard for him to talk about her. His goals are for her. After many goals, he points at the sky.
His mother says that after Celia died, Leo often talked to his grandmother, asking for help. He didn't tell much. He rarely talked about feelings.
Without his grandmother, he kept playing. He was still the best in his team. But something was wrong, and everyone could see it. The other children grew, he did not.
Newell's sent him to a hormone doctor, Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to know why its best young player was so much smaller.
Tests showed Lionel's body lacked growth hormone. Without medicine, he would be ten to fifteen centimetres shorter.
One word would keep following him. Small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: small injections in the leg, every night. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
From a young age, he learned to inject himself. Every night the same: a needle in his leg. A teammate once saw him do it before a game, as if it was normal.
A friend's father once taught him to drive on a quiet road. He was only eleven.
Every month, his father did the sums. The medicine took most of his factory salary. Help from insurance and the club stopped. Without treatment, his son's career would end before it began.
They looked for a club willing to pay. Lionel had a trial at River Plate, Buenos Aires, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026, Messi told the story himself. He trained for about ten days, and River wanted him to stay, even ready to pay for his medicine. But Newell's had to release him first.
That was the closest he came to a big club in his country.
But when he asked to be released, Newell's refused, and River's offer disappeared. That ended everything, he said. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona received a video of a boy from Rosario. With another agent, he took it to the club, and Barcelona invited him for a trial. In September 2000, Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's, his teammates didn't know where he had gone. The story was that he was ill.
In Barcelona, he played against older boys. Sporting director Carles Rexach was watching.
Supposedly the walk from Rexach's seat to the pitch takes only three or four minutes. He needed fifteen, because he kept staring at the boy.
One of the trialists was Cesc Fàbregas, later Messi's teammate. Before the game, the coach told him to mark the Argentine boy closely.
Cesc thought it would be easy. The boy was tiny. A moment later, Fàbregas was on the ground and the little one was gone with the ball.
Rexach says he told the club: sign him, don't think twice. But his bosses hesitated. The boy was a foreigner, very small and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed, no decision.
For Jorge, the waiting was hard. He had given up a steady job at the factory. He was living in a hotel in a foreign city with his son, not knowing if they could stay.
After more than two months, Jorge phoned Rexach and spoke firmly. If it wasn't settled soon, they would go home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met the agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. There was no paper, so he wrote a promise on a napkin. Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
A club director, Joan Gaspart, later admitted the napkin was not legally valid. It was a way to calm a father ready to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed it, two agents were witnesses. Later, the napkin sold at auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona would pay for the treatment and give his father a job. In February 2001, everyone moved to Spain.
At thirteen, Leo didn't yet understand what it meant. He only knew he would play, and the injections would continue, now paid for by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada, this was a dream. For his family, it was the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went as imagined. Because of foreign-player rules, Lionel couldn't play official games for months. And in his second game for the youth team, he broke his leg.
His mother, brothers and sister were homesick. They weren't happy in the new city, and within a year, decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back too. Lionel said no. Later he summed it up: I wanted to keep going, and my father stayed with me.
So the family was split across two continents. Lionel and his father in Barcelona. Part of Jorge's salary was for living there. The rest went to Rosario, for his wife and children.
Now a thirteen-year-old lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and sister.
Sundays were quiet. He played video games with his father in a small flat. Then, says his biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to his room and cried into his pillow.
My father was always by my side, says Messi, and we went through many bad things together.
At the club, he hardly spoke. At his first training, the coach asked his position. He mumbled "striker", then sat in the corner of the dressing room.
His teammates were puzzled. Fàbregas says for a long time they thought he couldn't speak. He could. He was just very shy. He didn't talk much. He just played.
He was nicknamed "el enano", the dwarf. But when he got the ball, nobody laughed.

Slowly he found his place. His team was full of boys born in 1987 like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three defenders and attacked all the time, until they were called the Baby Dream Team.
Slowly the quiet one started joking. It turned out he was funny, and liked cards and video games. He hated losing at those, just like at football.
One season, they hardly lost, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Tall Piqué looked after him.

Their coach, Tito Vilanova, later became an important person in Messi's life. Reportedly his team once led three-nil within three minutes. Tito joked to his assistant: what do we say at half-time if it's eight-nil?
Every night, the injections continued. Every year he grew a little more. By his teens, the treatment had worked.
He would end up around one metre seventy. Still among the smallest. But enough.
Later, his doctor in Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said frankly: he only helped the boy grow. The rest was Messi's own work.
In November 2003, Barcelona played a friendly in Porto, opening a new stadium. Frank Rijkaard brought on a sixteen-year-old youth player, Lionel Messi. On the opposing bench was José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly. But he had already played for the first team. That season he rose through four Barcelona teams in a row.
His official debut was on the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on late, wearing number thirty. He was seventeen.
At that time, he was Barcelona's youngest player in the Spanish league. The record was later broken by someone else. He then stayed at Barcelona for seventeen years.
Club people say off the pitch he was shy and almost silent. One agent said his legs were the skinniest he'd ever seen.
But someone in the dressing room saw his talent. Ronaldinho, the best player in the world, put his arm around the quiet boy.

Other Brazilian players, Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta, also looked after him. Ronaldinho sat next to him and invited him to eat at the Brazilian table. Leo learned a lot from them, he says, especially Ronaldinho.
Not everyone was so kind. Ludovic Giuly from France remembers some seniors kicking the boy in training, to test him. He didn't complain. He got up and kept playing.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on in the final minutes. Ronaldinho played a lofted pass and Messi chipped the ball over the keeper. The referee called offside.
Soon after, Ronaldinho did exactly the same thing again. Messi did exactly the same too. This time, the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down, the boy jumped on his back. It was his first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho says he is proud to have been there at the start of that story.

Let me pause the story for a moment. I'm Kamil, twenty-one. Since 2014, when I was nine, I've been making YouTube channels. Most failed. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver play button have been my dream since childhood. If this story means something to you, subscribing brings me one step closer. Back to the story.
In spring 2006, Barcelona were in the Champions League knockouts. Messi tore Chelsea apart at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, he tore a thigh muscle in the second leg. He went off crying.
The whole Camp Nou stood up and applauded. Rijkaard hugged him. Messi was only eighteen.
Barcelona then won the final in Paris. Messi didn't play. He was so sad he didn't join the celebrations. Later he said he deeply regretted that night.
In 2004, another issue arose. Messi had lived in Spain since thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him to play for Spain.
Argentina's youth coaches moved fast. In June 2004, they organised an Under-20 friendly against Paraguay, mainly so that Messi would play and be tied to his country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi says playing for Spain was possible. But in his heart, he was a Rosario boy.

Cesc Fàbregas, his best friend at the academy, said it would have been amazing if Leo had played for Spain. Later, Spain became world champions without him. Argentina's senior team still waited eleven more years for a trophy.
In 2005, at the Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was player of the tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina became world champions.
He also won the Golden Ball and Golden Boot: best player and top scorer. For the first time, the Rosario boy was a champion in the blue and white shirt.
Six weeks later, August 2005, he made his senior national team debut, in a friendly in Budapest against Hungary. He came on in the second half.

On his first touch, a defender pulled his shirt. Messi jerked his arm to get free, and his arm hit the defender. The referee showed him a red card. He hadn't been on the pitch a minute. Reportedly he left in tears.
Later he said: I came on, I was sent off, and they will never call me up again.
A teammate that night ran to protest to the referee for him. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember that name, because he comes back into this story later.
He was called up again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. That summer he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro, he came on and scored the sixth goal: six-nil. At eighteen, he was Argentina's youngest World Cup scorer.
He also gave an assist to Hernán Crespo. He already looked like he belonged there.
In the quarter-final against hosts Germany, Argentina were ahead. Then the last substitution was used on someone else, and the game slipped away. Argentina lost on penalties.
Messi was on the bench the whole game. For the first time, a World Cup ended while he only watched. He was silent in front of the press. Once again, he didn't say much.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi received the ball in his own half. He beat one, two, three players, then the keeper, and scored.
He started on the right near the halfway line. In ten seconds, he crossed almost the whole pitch, ball glued to his left foot.
All of Argentina recognised that goal. Almost the same as Diego Maradona's goal, Argentina's greatest hero, against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was only nineteen.
Barcelona won five-two. But in the second leg, Getafe won four-nil, Barcelona were knocked out. Even such a beautiful goal didn't save the team.
Those were hard years for Barcelona. Ronaldinho was fading, the team often lost, and the club was looking for a new start. Messi got better every month, but was often injured.
In the note after the 2026 final there is another sentence: I swear I always gave everything. That's true. But for a long time with Argentina, giving everything wasn't enough to win.
In summer 2007, at the Copa America in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi was only twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played the full game but could hardly do anything. He could only watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with the senior team. Nobody knew he would lose three more finals before winning.
In 2008, he wanted to play at the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona didn't want to release him, because the Olympics are not in the official football calendar. The case went to the sports court.
Messi said this was his choice, and an Olympic chance wouldn't come again. The court ruled for the club.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola. He had won Olympic gold in 1992 in Barcelona, and he understood. Messi was released.
There he scored against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.
In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand people, his pass sent his friend Ángel Di María through, who chipped the ball over the keeper. The only goal. Argentina won gold.
Later he said some things in football happen once in a lifetime. It was his only Olympics. He treasures that gold. And at Barcelona, Guardiola was ready to give him a new role.
Guardiola's first decision was a shock. Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, was no longer in his plans. Now Barcelona relied on a twenty-one-year-old.
That summer Ronaldinho went to Milan. Before leaving, he asked Leo to wear the number ten. The boy who once jumped on his back now wore it, and became the team's star.
In May 2009, Barcelona visited the Bernabéu to play Real Madrid. According to a book by journalist Martí Perarnau, the night before, Guardiola called Messi in and showed him a video.
Between Real's midfielders and defenders there was empty space. Guardiola told him to start on the right, then move into that space. When the ball comes, run straight at goal.
According to the book, Guardiola kept his plan secret until the end.
Messi was not a winger, not a striker. He was in between, and the defenders didn't know who should follow him. Barcelona won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored two.
Then, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were behind in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Iniesta, who scored. Barcelona reached the final.
Three weeks later in Rome, they met Manchester United in the Champions League final. Guardiola showed a video of their season, with music from Gladiator.
Before that final, Leo remembered Paris, the night he felt left out and stayed away from the party. This time, he said, he wanted to enjoy it more.
In the seventieth minute, Xavi crossed into the box. The smallest player jumped above the defenders and headed past the tall keeper Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar is almost two metres. Messi about one metre seventy. The boy who was too small won in the air.
Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won everything. League, cup, Champions League and three other trophies. Six out of six, never done by any team before.
The sixth trophy: December in Abu Dhabi, against Estudiantes from Argentina. In extra time, a Messi goal with his chest decided it.
Shortly before, he won his first Ballon d'Or, the title of best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who was too small was now number one.
In January 2011, at the Ballon d'Or night in Zurich, all three finalists came from the same school, Barcelona's academy, La Masia. Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Many backed Xavi or Iniesta. They had just become world champions with Spain, and Iniesta's goal won the final. But Messi won, two years in a row.
He said he didn't expect it. Xavi and Iniesta deserved it just as much, even more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three of them gave a press conference together, and all said: the award is for the team.
Later Xavi remembered meeting him while travelling: polite, humble, not arrogant. He hadn't expected that boy to become the best player in history.

In May 2011, at Wembley, Barcelona beat Manchester United again in the Champions League final. Messi scored with a hard shot from outside the box. The most emotional moment came at the end. That spring, a tumour had been removed from defender Éric Abidal's liver. Carles Puyol gave the captain's armband to Abidal, so he could lift the trophy.

In May 2012, Guardiola had his last home game at Barcelona. All four goals were scored by Messi. After the fourth, he ran to hug him. Guardiola joked that Leo stole the spotlight all season, and he couldn't be jealous.
In December 2012, he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in a year. Messi finished with ninety-one, five in one Champions League game.

Müller wasn't sulky. He called Leo a giant, and joked his only flaw was that he didn't play for Bayern. A few weeks later, Leo sent a Barcelona shirt with a handwritten note: with respect and admiration, a hug. For Leo, titles matter more than records.
His life off the pitch also changed. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, a Rosario girl he had known since childhood. In November 2012, their first son was born. His name was Thiago.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said becoming a father changes you completely. Now, he said, his son comes above everything.

In January 2013, he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. No one had won four before. But that winter, Tito Vilanova was back in cancer treatment. He had been his coach at La Masia, now with the first team. Abidal was also just recovering from a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich, Leo forgot to thank them. He then apologised. Tito, he said, believed in him when he still often sat on the bench.
At Barcelona, he was worshipped like a god. With the national team, it was a different story.
Argentina hadn't won a major trophy since 1993, when Messi was six. Now a whole country wanted him to end the wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina's coach was none other than Diego Maradona. In the quarter-final in Cape Town, Germany scored in the third minute and won four-nil. Messi didn't score a single goal.
After the game, Maradona said he saw Messi crying in the dressing room.
Those who say he doesn't love this shirt, Maradona said, are stupid.
Because that is what many Argentines said. He went to Spain at thirteen. He never played for an Argentine club. He didn't even sing the national anthem.
There was a term for players like him: "pecho frío". Cold chest. Not moved at important moments. For many, his silence meant he didn't care.
At the 2011 Copa America, in his own country, he was booed. His father said his son was very hurt, not understanding why he was jeered.
The coach at that Copa, Sergio Batista, used him as at Barcelona. It failed. Messi said comparing Argentina with Barcelona was wrong. Barcelona had played together for a long time.
Argentina were knocked out in the quarter-final, losing on penalties to Uruguay. The criticism kept coming. He stayed the same. He didn't say much. He just played.
In April 2014, Tito Vilanova died, aged forty-five. Six days earlier, according to Tito's assistant, Leo visited him and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried the team. After his first goal against Bosnia, he looked at the sky as usual. He scored four goals in the group, including the winner against Iran, in the ninety-first minute.
Four times he was player of the match. Argentina reached the final, the first in twenty-four years.
In the semi-final they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Defender Javier Mascherano said without Leo, Argentina wouldn't have got that far.
The final was at the Maracanã, Rio de Janeiro, again against Germany. Messi and his teammates had chances. No goal. Then in extra time, Mario Götze scored.
After the final whistle, Messi received the Golden Ball, best player of the tournament. When collecting it, he walked past the World Cup trophy without looking.
He didn't care about the Golden Ball, he said. The FIFA president at the time, Sepp Blatter, later said Messi kept repeating the same words: the best, but not champion.
A second lost final. Three years later he said this wound would never go away.
In 2015, at the Copa America in Chile, Argentina were back in the final. Against Chile, nil-nil after a hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed, and Chile won.
A month earlier, with Barcelona, he won the Champions League again in Berlin, with Neymar and Luis Suárez. With the club, he won everything. With the national team, he kept losing.
Chile's coach in that final was an Argentine, Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later, he coached Argentina.
Messi wrote that nothing in football hurts more than losing a final. Now it had happened three times.
In June 2016, there was one more chance. A special Copa America in the United States, a hundred years after the first. The final was at MetLife Stadium, near New York.
And the opponent was Chile, again. Again, no goals. Again, the game went to penalties.
Messi kicked first. He leaned back, and the ball flew high.
Chile won the shootout. It was his fourth lost final. Three years, three finals.
Lucas Biglia's penalty was also saved. But everyone remembers the captain's miss.
A few minutes later, in the tunnel, reporters stopped him. The quiet one said briefly: that's it, the national team is over for me.
His teammates were devastated. Sergio Agüero was his closest friend in the team. For years they almost always shared a room. Agüero said that defeat crushed Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a child, repeating: this isn't for me, this isn't for me.
That night, said the team's fitness coach, he found Leo still awake at two in the morning, sobbing.

Then something unexpected happened. In Argentina, people asked him to stay. The president phoned him, and said publicly that Messi was the greatest thing Argentina had. On a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires, hundreds of people with banners gathered at the Obelisk. "Don't go, Leo."
A fifteen-year-old boy, Enzo Fernández, also wrote to Leo asking him not to leave. Six years later, that boy played alongside him in a World Cup final.
The country that called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later, he returned and immediately scored.
Asked why he came back, he said he loved the country and this shirt too much, and wanted to help.
Later he explained the reason. It wasn't only the pain of losing, he said. Things outside football had hurt him and his family.
He also wasn't sure he had told his father before speaking in the tunnel. He just felt that at that moment it had to be that way.
That summer, a Spanish court convicted Messi and his father of tax fraud over image rights. Prison was replaced by a fine, common in Spain for first offences.
In court, Messi said his father handled the money. The family had already paid about five million euros.

In June 2017, Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city where they grew up. He could have married anywhere, but chose to go home. About two hundred and fifty guests came, including teammates from Barcelona and Argentina. Thiago and his little brother Mateo sat in front, and Leo's siblings were witnesses.

On the pitch, Argentina were in danger. Before the last 2018 World Cup qualifier, they were outside the qualifying places. They had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they hadn't won in sixteen years.

That night, Argentina's streets were nearly empty. People watched in bars and at home. In La Plata, the band U2 even delayed a concert so fans could watch on a giant screen. Then, in the first minute, Ecuador scored, and the bars went silent.
Then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three-one and qualified for Russia. Even Ecuador's fans applauded.
In the dressing room, the players sang for the critics. Mascherano said without the World Cup, many stories would have ended.
Messi said after the game it would have been crazy for Argentina to miss the World Cup. Now, he said, they were calm.
Coach Jorge Sampaoli's words are much remembered: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes him.
Russia did not pay it back. In the first game, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
The keeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, is also a film director. He said he had studied Messi's penalties.
Then a three-nil defeat to Croatia. Messi's goal beat Nigeria, and he said it was a huge relief.
In the round of sixteen, against France in Kazan, Antonela came with Thiago and Mateo, in shirts saying Papá. Argentina lost four-three. Messi went home with nothing again.

In the 2026 note, he also wrote that leaving the national team was a painful decision, and still painful, deep in his soul. He had felt it at Barcelona. There, the end began on some European nights the club would like to forget.

Everything began to crack. In 2018, they easily beat Roma in the first leg, then lost three-nil in Rome. A year later it happened again: won three-nil against Liverpool, then lost four-nil in Liverpool.
After Anfield, he said the coach wasn't to blame. He and his teammates, he said, were most to blame.
In 2019, he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, a record. But it couldn't mend what was cracked.
And in August 2020, in Lisbon, Bayern Munich thrashed Barcelona eight-two.
Ten days after Lisbon, Messi sent an official letter to the club. He wanted to leave. Barcelona refused, his contract didn't allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to talk. In the end Messi stayed a year, because he didn't want to sue his beloved club.
Six weeks after Lisbon, Barcelona let Luis Suárez go, one of his best friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a proper farewell, not to be kicked out. But nothing surprised him any more, he wrote.
Then, in November 2020, Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned for days. The man who once defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still hadn't won with Messi.
That year, the world was locked down by the pandemic. And in summer 2021, the Copa America was moved to Brazil at the last moment. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic, the stadium was almost empty. One of his biggest games with Argentina was played in silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, the captain who rarely spoke stood up. Someone filmed it.
For a long time people said he was too quiet to lead. That night, he spoke up.

Forty-five days without seeing family, guys, he said. He talked about keeper Emiliano Martínez, who had just become a father and hadn't yet held his daughter. Then: let's play confident and calm, because we're taking this cup home.
Martínez later said he wanted to cry. Another player said a moment later he was already crying, and didn't remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute, Rodrigo De Paul played a long ball to Ángel Di María, the friend who received Messi's pass at the Olympics. Di María chipped the ball over the keeper. One-nil.
For the next seventy minutes, Brazil attacked, Argentina defended. Messi missed a chance to add a goal. It didn't matter.
At the final whistle, Messi knelt and covered his face. His teammates ran and piled on top of him, until he vanished beneath them.
Then he phoned his wife and children in Rosario. After losing four finals, he was finally a champion with the senior team. He was thirty-four.
Di María said the curse had to break one day, and finally it did. Messi dedicated the title to his family, the Argentine people and Maradona, who surely supported them, wherever he is.
A month later, he was supposed to sign a new contract at Barcelona. But because of debts and Spanish league rules, the club couldn't afford to keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021, he walked into a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before he could speak, he cried.
He said he wasn't ready. He and his family wanted to stay. Arriving at thirteen, he left at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born there.
He was also sad he couldn't say goodbye to the fans in the stadium. Because of the pandemic, they hadn't met for a year and a half.
He moved to Paris Saint-Germain, but wasn't happy. When they lost, fans booed him.
Once, after a defeat, he flew to Saudi Arabia for a promotion without the club's permission. Paris suspended him, he apologised in a video. Everyone knew he wouldn't stay.

In November 2022, Argentina arrived at the World Cup in Qatar unbeaten in thirty-six games. The coach was Lionel Scaloni, who had defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew this might be his last chance.
In the first game, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. Then Saudi scored two goals in five minutes. Argentina lost two-one. One of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
After the game, Messi spoke to the press. No excuses, he said. The dressing room felt dead. He asked Argentines to trust the team: we will be more united than ever.
The players said he spoke more and more. The quiet captain now led out loud.
One song accompanied them. Fans called it Muchachos. The players sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, Messi joined in.
From then on, every game was a final. Messi opened the scoring against Mexico, a two-nil win. Then Poland and Australia fell.
Against Australia, his thousandth career game, he scored.
In the quarter-final, Argentina led the Netherlands two-nil, who equalised two-two in the final seconds. On penalties, Argentina won.
After the game, the world saw a different Messi. During a TV interview, a Dutch player walked past, and Messi said in Rosario street style: "What are you looking at, stupid?"

The one once labelled cold was now on fire. In the semi-final, Argentina beat Croatia three-nil. Messi scored a penalty, then beat one of the best young defenders in the world and set up Julián Álvarez's goal.
On the eighteenth of December 2022, Argentina met France in the final. Messi scored a penalty. Di María added a goal.
Two-nil, ten minutes left. Four lost finals behind him, the trophy in front of his eyes.
Then, in under two minutes, Kylian Mbappé scored two goals. Two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored again, three-two. Then Mbappé again, from a penalty. Three-three.
In the last minute, France had one chance, but Emiliano Martínez's leg saved it. A hundred and twenty minutes over, on to penalties.
Messi's penalty went in. Martínez saved one, France missed another. Then it was Gonzalo Montiel's turn, the deciding penalty.
This is the moment from the start of the film. Montiel steps up to the ball. Messi looks at the sky, and later said he begged God to end it.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi knelt on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had once said he was finished. He came back. Now at thirty-five, he was world champion.
Before he lifted the trophy, the Emir of Qatar put a traditional black robe on him. He lifted the cup, kissed it, and wouldn't let it go.
His family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran over. He took a photo of Antonela with the trophy.
In the final, he scored his sixth and seventh goals. He again won the Golden Ball, which eight years earlier he didn't care about because Argentina lost. This time, he held the trophy too.
In Qatar, he was the first to score in the group stage, round of sixteen, quarter-final, semi-final and final.
Later, on TV, he said the cup seemed to call to him: now you may touch me.
He has never rewatched the final, only highlights. At home, his son copies keeper Emiliano Martínez's celebration.
In Buenos Aires, millions filled the streets. There were so many that the team bus couldn't move, and players were flown out by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had one more happy night in Buenos Aires. In the first home game as world champions, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored his eight-hundredth goal. He had always dreamed of this: celebrating with his people, at home.
That summer, when his Paris contract ended, his choice surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not a giant Saudi offer. A young American club, Inter Miami. Many thought he went there to relax.
The reason was simple. He wanted to step a little away from the spotlight, and think more about family. If it were about money, he said, he would have gone to Saudi Arabia.
His Miami debut, July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one-one, his free kick curled into the top corner.
That night, he smiled from the bench towards Antonela and his three sons. LeBron James and Serena Williams were also watching. When the ball went in, the club owner, David Beckham, cried.
Soon Miami won the first trophy in its history. He said he wanted to relax. In October, he won his eighth Ballon d'Or too.
In Miami, he also became a supporter father. His three sons joined the club's academy. He and Antonela cheered at the side of the pitch, like other parents.
In 2024, Argentina reached the Copa America final again, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half, he sprained his ankle and had to go off.
On the bench, he cried. Teammate Leandro Paredes sat next to him. He couldn't look at him, only hear him crying. Argentina won in extra time without him. It was also Di María's last game.

In September 2025, he played what might be his last home World Cup qualifier, against Venezuela in Buenos Aires. In the warm-up, he held back tears as more than eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored two goals. Ending like this, at home, was his dream.
In December 2025, Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch, his son Mateo played with the ball, then pointed at his father.
In March 2026, he scored his nine-hundredth goal. He was thirty-eight, some said too old.
That goal came when Miami failed to win and were knocked out of the continental cup. For him, the result mattered more. And the World Cup was near.
His father, Jorge, always wanted to see him play in one more World Cup. But before the tournament, Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time, Jorge would not be there to watch him.
In the first game, against Algeria, he scored three. Then two against Austria, and one against Jordan. Argentina won the group easily.
And after every game, always the same. Boots off. Phone out. Any message from home? That's how he got news of his father.
He was silent, but he played while his father was ill, thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted he never felt good during the tournament.
In the knockouts every game was hard. Against Cape Verde, it went to extra time.
Against Egypt, Messi missed a penalty. Not hanging his head, he set up Cristian Romero's goal, the equaliser, then Enzo Fernández headed the winner. Against Switzerland, extra again.
Boots off. Phone out. Any message?

Semi-final in Atlanta, against England. England went ahead first. Argentina turned it around in the last five minutes, Messi's late pass became the winning goal. Two-one. They were in the final again.
When the game ended, Messi was overwhelmed with emotion. He went round the pitch hugging teammates and staff. Coach Scaloni too was lost for words.
He scored eight goals at that tournament. No player has scored more goals, or played more games, at the World Cup.
The final was played on the nineteenth of July 2026, at MetLife Stadium, New Jersey. The stadium where, ten years earlier, he said he was finished.
Before the game, in the dressing room, he asked his teammates to be calm, forget everything, and just think about playing.
Spain had Lamine Yamal, nineteen, and a young team. They controlled the ball and almost all the chances.
Still nil-nil. In a video released later, Messi is heard shouting: character, everyone, character.
At the end of normal time, Enzo Fernández, the boy who wrote the letter, was sent off. Ten men, thirty more minutes.
In the hundred-and-sixth minute, Ferran Torres scored. Argentina couldn't reply.
Messi had only one shot. It was his fifth lost final with Argentina.

After the final whistle, Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came and hugged him. Messi said, follow your own path, the future belongs to your generation. Yamal said those words were worth as much as a gold medal.
Scaloni cried at the press conference and had to leave. Before the final, he had said Messi was the best player there has ever been on a pitch.
The next day, Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is enormous, he said, and this wound needs time to heal.
Less than three weeks later, in August 2026, Jorge Messi died in Rosario after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
A few days later, Lionel wrote an open letter to him. It began simply: I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he had promised their father he would reach the final so that Dad could watch. His father didn't make it. Lionel wanted to win and bring the trophy to him. He couldn't, he wrote. His legs couldn't do any more.
He also wrote: after each World Cup game, he waited for his father's message. When no message came, he knew how bad things were.
You were my father, my best friend, my agent, he wrote. He was the one who once quit his job in Rosario and waited for a napkin in Barcelona.
Since then, in the sky he looks at, there are two people.
On the thirty-first of August, Messi posted the note from the start of this film. Written on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, then kept for six weeks.
In it, he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I have given everything. There is nothing more I can give, and great young players deserve to play. Now I am one of you.
He then added: today, after what happened to my father, I am even more sure of my decision.
He didn't write about trophies or finals. He wrote about family, the fans and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026, he played for Argentina for the last time, a friendly against Benin at the Monumental, Buenos Aires. River Plate's stadium, the club that once wanted the little boy from Rosario but couldn't have him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding his three sons' hands. His mother was in the stands.
The anthem was sung by Falklands War veterans. Messi held back tears. In the tenth minute, the game stopped for applause, and Benin's players came over to him.
He made two assists, then scored a penalty: his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in two hundred and eight games.
His second assist was for Nico Paz, twenty-two, a young player who he thinks deserves to play.
After the game, hundreds of drones lit up the sky. And the boy who once sat silent in the corner of the dressing room held the microphone, in front of eighty-five thousand people.
First, he said he was thinking of his father. Then, he said, this was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks, people argued about the referee of that World Cup. Messi didn't join in. That night he said there was nothing strange. His team just gave everything.
Playing for Argentina, he said, is the most beautiful thing for anyone. He wanted to be here all his life. Then he said he loved the fans and would miss them.
He went round with his wife and three sons, accompanied by eighty-five thousand voices: Messi isn't leaving.
He called it the saddest day of his career. But in the note he wrote: I leave in peace and proud.
He was too small. Too expensive. He was a foreigner in Spain and an outsider in Argentina. Later people said he was too old.
But two people disagreed. The grandmother who asked for him to be played. The father who earned the money, crossed the ocean and stayed.
He didn't play for himself, but for them. When he looks at the sky after a goal, they are who he is looking for.
The cold chest people talked about was never cold. He just didn't show it. He held it in and let it out when he lost, or finally won.
The last final, July 2026, hurt the most. It wasn't about one more trophy. It was the last thing he wanted to bring home for his father.
Today he is still in Miami. More than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. Now, as he wrote, he is just a fan.
Maybe you are the quiet one. The one in the corner of the dressing room. The one people think doesn't care.
Leo was that kid too. He never became loud. He doesn't talk much. He just plays, for those who believe in him. At the most important moments, he spoke up. One day, the world listened.
If you are quiet, you don't need to be loud. Keep playing. Your time to speak will come.
On his farewell night, the boy who was once quiet smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I've never talked this much, he said, I don't want to leave.
That year, Spain didn't only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, they buried the dream of another boy who also longed for it.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, once nicknamed crybaby by his teammates. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is here.
